spans.s:
Nada is found in several passages of the Rigveda, but its sense is still obscure. It is identified by Pischel with naḍa, being explained by him in one passage as a reed boat, which is split, and over which the waters go; in another as a reed whip, of which the sharp points (karṇa) are used to urge horses on; and in others again as figuratively designating the penis. Roth takes the sense to be ‘bull’ (either literally or meta phorically) in all passages. Once at least the ‘neigher’ (from the root nad, ‘sound’) seems to be meant with reference to Indra's horse. In the phrase nadasya karṇaiḥ^8 the sense is, perhaps, ‘through the ears of the (side) horse’ (that is, by their being ready to hear the word of command) of their chariot, the Maruts ‘hasten on with their swift steeds’ (turayanta āśubhiḥ).

Nadī, ‘stream,’ is mentioned in the Rigveda and later. Reference is made to shallows (gādha) in the river's bed, to the opposite bank (pāra), and to the bathing of horses in streams. Rivers are also mentioned in close connexion with mountains. The title nadī-pati, ‘lord of rivers,’ is once used to express ‘ocean’ or ‘sea-water.’
